labels.predict: Which supplied description will match the dog photograph best?
steps: Keep the photograph fixed. Read all three candidate descriptions and predict their order.
Run the experiment or view the recorded measurement. Read the cosine scores before the percentages.
Replace the menu with Newfoundland, pug, and Persian. Run live again; the model weights stay fixed.
labels.observe: The supplied dog description wins. A new candidate menu asks a new question using the same encoders.
labels.output: One matching score for each supplied description, sorted from highest to lowest.

attributes.predict: Can we ask what is inside the cup, rather than just name the cup?
steps: Compare the four drink/food descriptions with the coffee photograph.
Run and inspect the gap between coffee and tea.
Change only the descriptions to ask about a different property. Each new menu needs a live run.
attributes.observe: Coffee ranks above tea in this run. This is a choice among our descriptions, not a list of attributes generated by CLIP.
attributes.output: A ranking of the four supplied descriptions.

search.predict: What will a search for ‘something to drink’ return from this gallery?
steps: Read the query and look through the 22-image gallery. Predict the first three results.
Run and inspect the returned pictures, not just the first score.
Try ‘a laptop’, which is absent from this gallery. A nearest result still exists; decide whether it is relevant.
search.observe: The generated red and blue mugs precede the coffee photograph in the recorded browser run. The gallery and wording both matter.
search.output: All 22 gallery images ranked against one text query.

captions.predict: Which of these four complete sentences best matches the rocket photograph?
steps: Read the exact candidate sentences; these are inputs we supply.
Run and compare the best sentence with the distractors.
Remove the rocket sentence and rerun. CLIP can only rank the sentences still on the menu.
captions.observe: The rocket sentence wins here. CLIP selects a supplied sentence; it does not write a new caption.
captions.output: A score for each candidate sentence.

neighbors.predict: Which other gallery image will be nearest to the Persian cat photograph?
steps: Use the Persian cat as the query. Its own image is excluded from the results.
Run and inspect the top neighbors; similarity does not establish duplicate files.
Switch the query to the pug or a portrait. No text candidates are needed.
neighbors.observe: Chelsea is the nearest other image in this gallery. Related content can match even when the photographs differ.
neighbors.output: The other 21 gallery images ranked against the query image.

hat.predict: Which candidate word best describes the change between the two pictures?
steps: Read the Before and After labels. Predict a word before running.
Run and compare the signed change scores for hat, cup, cat, and boat.
Swap before / after and run again. With fixed candidates, every change score should reverse sign.
hat.change: A straw hat is added to the portrait.
hat.held: The person, pose, clothing, framing, and background are intended to stay the same.
hat.limits: These are generated pictures. Hair, lighting, and fine details can also change; the pair does not perfectly isolate a hat.
hat.observe: Hat has the largest positive change score in the recorded run. That is evidence for this pair and candidate list, not a general law of concept arithmetic.
hat.output: One signed cosine between the after − before direction and each candidate word.

competition.predict: What will win when none of the descriptions says ‘dog’?
steps: Keep the dog photograph and the deliberately wrong menu: cat, bird, car.
Run. Inspect the winning description and its raw cosine.
Add ‘a photo of a dog’ and rerun. The old pairwise cosines stay fixed, while their relative shares change.
competition.observe: Car wins the wrong menu in the browser recording. Highest among these choices does not mean correct.
competition.output: Scores and relative shares across the supplied menu, even if every option is wrong.

negation.predict: Will ‘a photo without a cat’ score much lower than ‘a photo of a cat’?
steps: Use the cat photograph with both the positive and negated descriptions.
Run and compare their raw scores, not just their ordering.
Try another phrasing while keeping the photograph fixed. Save failures as well as successes.
negation.observe: The positive and negated cat phrases are only about 0.004 apart in the browser recording. This example exposes a language limitation.
negation.output: A similarity for each complete phrase; no rule explicitly implements logical negation.

sustainability.predict: Which supplied scene description matches the generated kiln tile?
steps: Start with the kiln image and all four aerial-scene descriptions.
Run, then switch among kiln, solar farm, fields, and warehouses while keeping the menu fixed.
Compare ‘brick kiln’ with a longer description in a separate live run. Record the images and wording used.
sustainability.observe: The kiln description wins the default example. These generated scenes motivate a satellite-search task; they do not measure performance on real satellite data.
sustainability.output: Four scene-description scores for the selected synthetic aerial tile.

healthcare.predict: Can CLIP match this public radiograph to an imaging modality?
steps: Compare the four modality descriptions with the public chest radiograph.
Run and inspect the matching scores.
Keep the distinction clear: identifying an image type is a different task from diagnosing disease.
healthcare.observe: Chest X-ray wins this modality menu. No disease labels or diagnostic outcome are evaluated here.
healthcare.output: A ranking of image-type descriptions, not a diagnosis.

sketch.predict: Can the dog concept still match when the image is a pencil sketch?
steps: Classify the sketch with the four ‘a drawing of …’ candidates.
Switch to the generated photograph-style dog and rerun with the same candidates.
Open Style change to ask a different question: what changed between the two images?
sketch.observe: Dog wins the sketch example. Recognizing the subject and identifying a change in style are separate experiments.
sketch.output: One similarity per description for a single image; there is no subtraction in this example.

color-change.predict: Which word matches the change from the red mug to the blue mug?
steps: Use red as Before and blue as After. Keep blue, red, cup, and hat as the candidates.
Run. Compare blue with red, then ask why cup need not win even though both images contain a cup.
Swap before / after and run again. The scores reverse sign; the highest-ranked word may change.
color-change.change: The mug’s surface color changes from red to blue.
color-change.held: The mug shape, handle, position, viewpoint, tabletop, and background are intended to stay the same.
color-change.limits: Generated reflections, edges, and background details can differ too. The measured direction contains every encoded difference, not only color.
color-change.observe: Blue has a positive change score and red a negative one in the recorded run. Cup is near zero: a feature shared by both images may contribute little to their difference.
color-change.output: Signed matches to the change direction, not probabilities that an image contains a blue or red object.

chimney.predict: Which word matches the change between the two kiln scenes?
steps: Read Before and After: a chimney is added in the second generated scene.
Run against chimney, tree, truck, and solar panel.
Swap the order and rerun. Inspect the pictures for changed shadows and background details.
chimney.change: A tall brick chimney is added to a kiln scene.
chimney.held: The kiln, brick stacks, camera position, and surrounding landscape are intended to stay the same.
chimney.limits: The chimney brings a shadow; generated fine details also vary. This pair is not a verified physical intervention or a trained kiln detector.
chimney.observe: Chimney has the largest positive score here. The result belongs to this synthetic pair, not to an evaluation across real kiln sites.
chimney.output: A ranked match between the image-change direction and four words.

medical-change.predict: Will the added device make ‘pacemaker’ the highest-scoring word?
steps: Compare the two generated radiograph-style pictures. The second adds a pacemaker-like object and leads.
Run with all four candidates unchanged. Keep the observed result even if it is surprising.
Try fuller descriptions in a separate run. Record the original failure alongside any improvement.
medical-change.change: A pacemaker-like device and leads are added to a synthetic radiograph-style image.
medical-change.held: The chest outline, viewpoint, and radiograph appearance are intended to stay the same.
medical-change.limits: Both images are generated; anatomy and device placement are approximate, and other pixels differ. This is not a patient before/after study.
medical-change.observe: Hat ranks first in the recorded q8 browser run; pacemaker does not. The intended edit is a hypothesis, not a guaranteed output.
medical-change.output: Four exploratory word scores for a synthetic change; no clinical finding is inferred.

style-change.predict: Does the change direction emphasize pencil sketch, photograph, dog, or cat?
steps: Use the photograph-style dog as Before and the pencil sketch as After.
Run with the four candidate words fixed. Contrast the style word with the subject word.
Swap the order and rerun. Then use Photo → sketch to classify each image separately.
style-change.change: A photograph-style dog scene is rendered as a pencil sketch.
style-change.held: The dog identity, pose, and composition are intended to remain similar.
style-change.limits: Color, texture, background, and small shapes all change. This direction does not isolate a single style coordinate.
style-change.observe: Pencil sketch wins; dog is near zero in the recorded difference. That does not mean the sketch contains no dog: the dog is shared by both pictures.
style-change.output: A signed match to the style-change direction, distinct from recognizing the dog in either image.
